name: Cyber awareness question bank
about: 40 behaviour questions from the Cyber team. Each has four options, one correct answer and an explanation. 16 questions match a phase of the attack story (phase_id); the rest are general and can be used at any checkpoint (phase_id is null). related_controls lists the controls in challenge.json that deal with the same risk as the question. Training and awareness (P5) relates to every question.

tiers.label: Spot the Risk
tiers.meaning: Recognise an obvious risk or warning sign.

tiers.label: Read the Signs
tiers.meaning: Notice context, clues and unsafe workarounds.

tiers.label: Choose Your Response
tiers.meaning: Apply a secure behaviour in a realistic workplace situation.

tiers.label: Pressure Test
tiers.meaning: Maintain secure behaviour under trust, urgency, authority or social pressure.

questions.question: You receive an email asking you to confirm your password to avoid losing access to your account. What is the biggest warning sign?

options.A: The email has a company logo
options.B: The sender asks for your password
options.C: The email contains text
options.D: The email arrives in the morning

questions.explanation: Legitimate organisations should never ask you to reveal your password by email. Requests for passwords are a common phishing technique used to gain access to accounts.

questions.question: You receive an email that appears to come from a supplier asking you to review an attached invoice you were not expecting. What should you do?

options.A: Open the attachment immediately
options.B: Forward it to colleagues for advice
options.C: Pause and verify the request before opening the attachment
options.D: Reply asking if it's genuine

questions.explanation: Unexpected attachments should always be treated with caution. Verifying before opening helps prevent malware infections and phishing attacks.

questions.question: You are covering for a colleague and receive an urgent invoice approval request shortly before a deadline. The sender appears legitimate but you were not expecting the request. What should you do?

options.A: Approve it to avoid delays
options.B: Verify the request through an independent channel first
options.C: Forward it to your entire team
options.D: Delete it immediately

questions.explanation: Business pressures and deadlines can encourage quick decisions. Taking time to verify unusual requests helps prevent fraud and phishing attacks.

questions.question: You receive an email from your manager requesting an urgent payment approval. The email references a genuine project, uses your manager's usual writing style and states the supplier must be paid within the next hour. What should you do?

options.A: Approve the payment immediately
options.B: Forward it to Finance
options.C: Verify the request using a trusted method before taking action
options.D: Reply asking for more information

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because it combines urgency, familiarity and genuine business context. Attackers often mimic trusted individuals and real projects to bypass normal verification processes.

questions.question: A colleague tells you they use the same password for several websites. What is the main risk?

options.A: The password is easier to remember
options.B: If one account is compromised, multiple accounts may be affected
options.C: The password may expire
options.D: It reduces internet speed

questions.explanation: Using different passwords for different accounts limits the impact of a single compromise and helps protect personal and work accounts.

questions.question: A colleague messages you saying they cannot access an urgent system and asks you to send your password so they can complete a task before a deadline. What should you do?

options.A: Refuse and direct them to the correct support process
options.B: Log in yourself and let them use your session
options.C: Send your password to help them
options.D: Share part of your password

questions.explanation: Passwords should never be shared, even with trusted colleagues. Individual accounts provide accountability and help protect systems and information. Colleagues should use approved support channels to resolve access issues.

questions.question: A colleague cannot access a system and asks if they can quickly sign in using your account to finish an urgent task. What should you do?

options.A: Allow them to use your account
options.B: Share your password verbally
options.C: Refuse and direct them to the correct support process
options.D: Log in for them and walk away

questions.explanation: Sharing accounts removes accountability and can create security risks. Everyone should use their own authorised access.

questions.question: You receive a Teams message from someone claiming to be IT Support. They know your manager's name, employee number and office location. They ask you to confirm your password reset details. What should you do?

options.A: Provide the requested information
options.B: Share part of the information
options.C: Verify the request independently and do not share passwords
options.D: Ignore all future IT communications

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because the individual knows genuine information that creates trust. Legitimate support teams do not need your password, and identity should always be verified independently.

questions.question: You receive an MFA approval request on your phone that you were not expecting. What should you do?

options.A: Approve it quickly
options.B: Ignore or deny the request and investigate if necessary
options.C: Approve it later
options.D: Forward it to a colleague

questions.explanation: Unexpected MFA prompts can indicate somebody is attempting to access your account. Never approve a request you did not initiate.

questions.question: You receive an unexpected MFA prompt, decline it, and no further prompts appear. What should you do?

options.A: Ignore it because the prompts stopped
options.B: Approve the next prompt if it appears
options.C: Change your password immediately without reporting it
options.D: Report the unexpected MFA request through the appropriate process

questions.explanation: Unexpected MFA prompts may indicate someone is attempting to access your account. Even if the prompts stop, reporting suspicious activity helps security teams investigate and protect accounts.

questions.question: You are working on an urgent task when several MFA prompts appear unexpectedly on your device. What should you do?

options.A: Approve one to stop the notifications
options.B: Ignore them and continue working
options.C: Treat them as suspicious, do not approve and report them
options.D: Switch MFA off

questions.explanation: Unexpected MFA requests can indicate attempted account compromise. Convenience should never override secure behaviour.

questions.question: A caller claiming to be technical support explains they are fixing an issue affecting your account. While on the call, an MFA request appears and they ask you to approve it so they can continue. What should you do?

options.A: Approve it because they called first
options.B: Approve it if they know your details
options.C: Refuse, verify independently and only approve requests you personally initiate
options.D: Approve it once and change your password later

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because the caller appears helpful and creates urgency. Attackers frequently use MFA fatigue and social engineering to gain account access. Only approve requests connected to your own actions.

questions.question: You receive a text message claiming to be from your bank asking you to click a link to verify your account. What is the biggest warning sign?

options.A: The message contains a link
options.B: The message arrives on your phone
options.C: The message uses your name
options.D: The message contains text

questions.explanation: Unexpected messages asking you to click links or provide information should be treated with caution. Criminals often use text messages to lead people to fake websites.

questions.question: You receive a text message claiming a parcel delivery has failed and asks you to pay a small fee using a provided link. What should you do?

options.A: Pay the fee immediately
options.B: Click the link to investigate
options.C: Forward the message to friends
options.D: Verify the delivery through a trusted source before taking action

questions.explanation: Unexpected messages often create urgency to encourage quick decisions. Using trusted sources helps avoid scams and protects personal information.

questions.question: You receive a phone call from someone claiming to be from IT Support. They explain there is a problem with your account and ask you to provide information to help them resolve it. What should you do?

options.A: Provide the information requested
options.B: Verify the caller's identity through official channels before sharing information
options.C: Ask them to call back later and then provide the details
options.D: Share only part of the information

questions.explanation: Phone calls can be used to build trust and obtain sensitive information. Always verify identities before sharing information or taking action.

questions.question: A caller claims to be from IT Support and knows your manager's name, department and recent project. They explain an urgent security issue is affecting your account and ask you to confirm account details immediately. What should you do?

options.A: Provide the information because they know internal details
options.B: Share limited information to help them investigate
options.C: Verify the request independently before sharing any information
options.D: Ask a colleague what they would do and then comply

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because the caller appears credible and uses genuine information to build trust. Attackers often combine urgency and familiarity to persuade people to bypass verification processes.

questions.question: A colleague recommends a free mobile app that makes work tasks faster, but it is not an approved company application. What should you do?

options.A: Check whether the app is approved before using it for work
options.B: Install the app because it improves productivity
options.C: Install it temporarily and remove it later
options.D: Ask colleagues whether they use it and follow their lead

questions.explanation: Only approved applications should be used for company work. Unapproved software can introduce security, privacy or compliance risks.

questions.question: While travelling, you see a QR code offering free access to airport Wi-Fi. What should you do?

options.A: Scan it immediately
options.B: Verify that the Wi-Fi service and QR code are legitimate before using them
options.C: Install software suggested by the QR code
options.D: Use any website the QR code opens

questions.explanation: Criminals sometimes replace legitimate QR codes with malicious versions. Verifying the source helps prevent phishing and malware attacks.

questions.question: You are attending a conference and a QR code is displayed to access event materials. The session is about to start and attendees are already scanning it. What should you do?

options.A: Scan it immediately because everyone else is doing so
options.B: Ignore all conference QR codes
options.C: Take a photo and share it online
options.D: Check that it belongs to the event organiser before using it

questions.explanation: Even in legitimate settings, it is good practice to verify links before using them. Social pressure should not replace good judgement.

questions.question: A colleague sends you a QR code in a Teams chat saying it provides immediate access to a shared project folder needed for an urgent meeting. The colleague appears genuine and the project is real. What should you do?

options.A: Scan the code immediately
options.B: Use the QR code because the project is genuine
options.C: Verify the source and destination before accessing the content
options.D: Forward the QR code to the whole team

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because it involves a genuine colleague, real project and time pressure. Attackers often exploit trusted channels to encourage quick decisions without verification.

questions.question: A stranger asks questions about your workplace and internal systems. What should you do?

options.A: Share information to be helpful
options.B: Provide only publicly available information
options.C: Be cautious about sharing internal information
options.D: Answer all questions politely

questions.explanation: Social engineering often starts with gathering information. Seemingly harmless details can be used to support future attacks.

questions.question: You overhear someone encouraging colleagues to bypass a security process because it takes too long. What should you do?

options.A: Ignore the conversation
options.B: Follow the shortcut because others are doing it
options.C: Suggest additional shortcuts
options.D: Challenge the behaviour appropriately or report the concern through the correct channel

questions.explanation: Security controls are in place to protect people, systems and information. Concerns about bypassing controls should be challenged or reported appropriately.

questions.question: You are approached by a visitor who appears lost and asks if you can let them into the building using your pass. They seem friendly and professional. What should you do?

options.A: Provide detailed information and directions
options.B: Do not let them enter using your pass. Direct them to reception or security and follow local access procedures
options.C: Escort them everywhere they ask to go
options.D: Give them a company directory

questions.explanation: Friendly interactions can still be used to gain unauthorised access. Situational awareness helps balance helpfulness with security.

questions.question: A contractor working on a legitimate project knows several colleagues by name and asks questions about systems, processes and security arrangements. They explain the information will help them complete their work more quickly. What should you do?

options.A: Provide the information because they are working on a genuine project
options.B: Give high-level answers only
options.C: Assume approval has already been granted
options.D: Verify they have a legitimate business need to know before sharing information

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because the request involves a genuine contractor and legitimate business activity. Attackers can exploit trust and familiarity to gather information that can support future attacks.

questions.question: You notice a colleague has left their laptop unlocked while away from their desk. What is the main security risk?

options.A: The battery may run out
options.B: Someone could access information or systems using the device
options.C: The device may go to sleep
options.D: The device may disconnect from Wi-Fi

questions.explanation: Unlocked devices can provide unauthorised access to information, systems and accounts. Locking devices helps protect company information.

questions.question: You notice someone following closely behind employees through a secure door without using an access badge. What should you do?

options.A: Ignore it because someone else let them in
options.B: Challenge politely or follow local security procedures
options.C: Hold the door open for them
options.D: Assume they are authorised

questions.explanation: Secure areas rely on access controls. Tailgating can allow unauthorised individuals to enter restricted locations.

questions.question: You are working in an office and step away for a short meeting. Several documents containing business information are visible on your desk. What should you do?

options.A: Leave them visible because you will be back soon
options.B: Store or secure sensitive information before leaving
options.C: Ask a colleague to watch the desk
options.D: Turn the documents upside down

questions.explanation: Good physical security includes protecting information from unnecessary exposure. A clear desk helps reduce accidental disclosure.

questions.question: A visitor carrying equipment arrives at a secure office entrance. They know a colleague's name, appear professional and explain they are running late for an important meeting. They ask you to hold the door so they do not need to sign in again. What should you do?

options.A: Allow them in because they appear legitimate
options.B: Let them in if they know a colleague's name
options.C: Follow visitor access procedures and ensure they use the proper sign-in process
options.D: Ask whether they promise to sign in later

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because the visitor appears genuine and creates urgency. Physical security controls are effective only when procedures are followed consistently.

questions.question: You accidentally send an email containing business information to the wrong recipient. What should you do first?

options.A: Report the incident through the appropriate process as soon as possible
options.B: Wait to see if the recipient notices
options.C: Delete the email from your Sent Items
options.D: Send another email asking the recipient to ignore it and take no further action

questions.explanation: Mistakes can happen. Prompt reporting allows appropriate action to be taken quickly and helps reduce the impact of a potential information security incident.

questions.question: A colleague is working from home and cannot access a company system. They ask if you can send a report containing customer information to their personal email account so they can finish an urgent task. What should you do?

options.A: Send it immediately
options.B: Upload it to a free file-sharing site
options.C: Send part of the information
options.D: Use approved company methods only

questions.explanation: Using approved company methods helps protect sensitive information and ensures the appropriate security controls remain in place.

questions.question: You are preparing a presentation for a management meeting and discover a spreadsheet containing employee personal information attached to your working files. The meeting starts in 15 minutes and colleagues are waiting for the final version. What should you do?

options.A: Leave the spreadsheet attached because you are short on time
options.B: Review whether the information is needed and remove unnecessary personal data before sharing
options.C: Send the presentation and explain the issue later
options.D: Share the spreadsheet separately so everyone has the same information

questions.explanation: Deadlines should not override good information-handling practices. Only information that is genuinely needed should be shared.

questions.question: A trusted colleague working on a genuine project urgently requests sensitive information and says approval has already been given. You cannot verify this. What should you do?

options.A: Send the information because the project is genuine
options.B: Send part of the information
options.C: Verify approval through the appropriate process before sharing
options.D: Assume approval exists and proceed

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because it involves a genuine colleague, project and business need. Attackers often use urgency and trust to encourage people to bypass normal controls.

questions.question: Which information should generally not be shared publicly online?

options.A: Favourite football team
options.B: Holiday photos
options.C: Internal company information
options.D: Favourite food

questions.explanation: Information shared publicly can be used by attackers to learn about an organisation or individual and support future attacks.

questions.question: Someone claiming to work for a supplier contacts you on LinkedIn. They ask what security tools your organisation uses so they can understand compatibility requirements. What should you do?

options.A: Share the information because they appear professional
options.B: Ignore all LinkedIn messages
options.C: Avoid sharing internal information and verify the request through appropriate channels
options.D: Add them to company groups

questions.explanation: Professional networking platforms can be used for information gathering. Internal information should only be shared through approved and verified channels.

questions.question: You are updating your professional networking profile and want to highlight projects you have worked on since joining the company. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Share only information approved for public release and keep internal details private
options.B: List confidential projects but avoid naming the company
options.C: Include details of technologies, suppliers and internal systems
options.D: Upload screenshots of project dashboards

questions.explanation: Professional profiles should balance personal achievements with protecting sensitive company information.

questions.question: Someone on a professional networking platform has mutual contacts, appears genuine and knows information about your organisation. They ask questions about internal systems and security arrangements. What should you do?

options.A: Answer because they appear legitimate
options.B: Share high-level details only
options.C: Verify the purpose and avoid sharing information that could assist an attacker
options.D: Connect first and answer later

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because the individual appears credible and has genuine connections. Attackers often use trust and familiarity to gather information gradually.

questions.question: A security tool on your device is preventing an application from running correctly. What should you do?

options.A: Follow the appropriate support process rather than disabling the security control
options.B: Ask a colleague how they bypassed the control
options.C: Disable the security tool so the application works
options.D: Uninstall the security tool permanently

questions.explanation: Security controls should not be disabled without proper authorisation. If a tool causes a problem, use the approved support process so the issue can be investigated safely.

questions.question: Your train is delayed and you need to submit an urgent report. A free public Wi-Fi network appears with a name that looks legitimate. What should you do?

options.A: Connect immediately because the report is urgent
options.B: Use approved secure access methods, such as a VPN where required
options.C: Disable security software to improve connectivity
options.D: Send the report before checking the connection

questions.explanation: Urgency should not override secure working practices. Public networks should be approached cautiously and used according to company guidance.

questions.question: You are working in a busy airport lounge and need to review a report containing sensitive business information before an important meeting. What should you do?

options.A: Continue working normally because nobody appears interested
options.B: Take steps to reduce visibility of sensitive information and remain aware of your surroundings
options.C: Increase screen brightness so the report is easier to read
options.D: Send the report to your personal device to review later

questions.explanation: Situational awareness is important when working in public. Information can be exposed through shoulder surfing and other risks.

questions.question: You are in a hotel. The Wi-Fi appears genuine, colleagues are already connected and you urgently need access to company systems before an important meeting. What should you do?

options.A: Connect because others are already using it
options.B: Bypass security controls because it is urgent
options.C: Follow approved secure access methods and verify the network before accessing sensitive information
options.D: Use the same password for personal and work services

questions.explanation: This scenario is difficult because urgency and social proof make the situation appear safe. Secure access procedures should still be followed even when time pressure exists.
